scale: -2 strongly disagree, -1 disagree, 0 argued neutral (three EUvox cases or vote/statement contradiction), +1 agree, +2 strongly agree, null = no public position found. Positions are the party's relative to the statement text as written.

evidence_tiers.3: party's own questionnaire answer (Greenpeace, NZCTU, Grey Power, KPMG tracker)
evidence_tiers.5: coalition agreement or government action attributable to the party (flagged)

statements.text: The government should take active steps to reduce the gap between high and low incomes, even if that means higher taxes for some people.

national.evidence: No 2026 text on narrowing the income gap; National's fiscal plan rules out 'new taxes' and attacks Labour/Greens/TPM 'nine new taxes' as punishing 'Kiwis who do the right thing and save and invest' (Fiscal Plan, Oct 2026). Inference from explicit general principle (no higher taxes) -> disagree; recorded as inference.

labour.evidence: 2026 CGT (28% on property gains) ring-fenced for health, pay-equity restoration and Living Wage across the public service; Labour frames CGT as fairness between work and property income. No explicit 'reduce the gap' pledge or broad higher taxes (rules out wealth tax).

green.evidence: Tax policy 2026 'A tax system for all of us': 2.5% tax on net assets over $10m, capital acquisitions tax, higher corporate tax and new top income rate 'to address inequality' and cut income tax for 96%.

act.evidence: Fiscal Plan 2026 cuts spending to 2017 per-person levels and rules out new taxes; Seymour (CA ANZ forum, 21 Sep 2026): the problem is public-sector productivity, 'not too little revenue'; ACT campaigns against wealth/asset taxes as 'envy taxes'. Emphasised rejection of higher taxes for redistribution.

nz-first.evidence: Peters attacks 'neoliberal' asset sales and wants a state bank, higher minimum wage with inflation and a $70 In-Work Tax Credit rise, but also calls TOP's/Greens' wealth taxes 'communism' (13 Sep 2026) and proposes a 20% SME tax rate. Both sides emphasised -> argued neutral.

te-pati-maori.evidence: 'A Kiwi Tax Plan' (26 Aug 2026): first $30,000 tax-free, 48% top rate above $300,000, tiered wealth tax from 1.5% on net wealth over $2m, higher corporate tax - explicitly to shift the burden to wealth and high incomes.

opportunity.evidence: Tax Reset (May 2026): Citizens' Income, 'lifting at least 50,000 families out of poverty', funded by a 1.75% land value tax and three-rate income tax (39% above $200k); redistributive but framed as broad tax cut, so qualified.

animal-justice.evidence: People policies address 'economic inequality' and reducing inequality through employment law and transition support; no tax policy stated. Qualified, low.

alliance.evidence: Tax Justice policy (Sep 2026): first $20,000 tax-free funded by a 2.5% wealth tax over $2m, 47% top rate above $250,000; 'income is taxed from the first dollar... while wealth is lightly taxed'.

conservative.evidence: Finance policy: 'press for a flat tax rate for individuals and for companies'; principles: New Zealanders 'free to enjoy the fruits of their labour to the greatest possible extent'. Explicit principle against redistributive taxation; qualified.

womens-rights.evidence: 'Minimum wages and benefits need to be increased so that all people have living incomes'; CPAG-style Working for Families reform for 'the poorest families'. No tax measure; qualified, low.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Universal Whānau Allowance, debt amnesty, 25% mana whenua equity in regional infrastructure, living-wage trade academy - redistribution without a stated tax measure; qualified, low.

statements.text: Lower taxes do more good for New Zealand than more government spending, even if it means fewer public services.

national.evidence: Fiscal Plan (Oct 2026): 'not impose new taxes', 'show ongoing restraint so that overall government expenditure comes down towards 30% of GDP', 'right-sizing government'; but also pledges to 'continue investing in health, schools, law and order' - so a qualified preference for lower tax/smaller state.

labour.evidence: Fiscal Strategy 2026: 'balance the books without shrinking the economy'; funds Medicard, free prescriptions and public-service restoration partly through a new CGT; attacks National's tax cuts 'to those at the top'. Prefers services over tax cuts, qualified.

green.evidence: Greens fund free ECE, dental, fees-free and public housing by taxing 'the super-rich and large corporates'; manifesto: 'fund public services adequately'; Green Budget 2025 raises revenue and borrowing rather than cutting.

act.evidence: Fiscal Plan 2026: 'reducing spending to 2017 levels adjusted for wages, inflation and population', cut new spending from $2.4b to $2b, consolidate 43 departments to 19; balancethebooks.nz: 'ACT will pay down debt faster'; tax cuts funded from smaller government.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Manifesto 2026 doubles baseline benefits, free GP and dental care, free public transport, $1b Pūngao Auaha fund, funded by wealth and corporate taxes - more spending and higher taxes on the wealthy.

opportunity.evidence: Tax Reset shifts tax onto land to fund a universal income and keeps revenue; infrastructure policy to borrow for $60b of investment; 10-year health plan lifting funding to 9% of GDP. Opposes smaller-state framing; qualified.

nz-loyal.evidence: 'Scrap the current tax system' and 'reject government overreach' (website via RNZ); replacement not described. Weak inference toward smaller state, low.

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: 'Smaller, leaner central government', 'Ending Bureaucratic Waste', shrink central ministries; no tax-cut pledge. Qualified, low.

alliance.evidence: Free GP, dental, optical and audiology care, universal child benefit, free public transport, funded by wealth, CGT and transaction taxes; 'reverse privatisation'. Public services over tax cuts.

conservative.evidence: Small Government page: 'over-governed, over-regulated, and over-taxed'; 'Government spending and borrowing... must be slashed'; cut personal and company tax, GST to 12.5%; 'shrink government so that it focuses on its core business'.

statements.text: Gains people make from rising property and asset values should be taxed in the same way as income from work.

national.evidence: 'No new taxes, including no capital gains tax' (Fiscal Plan, Oct 2026); Luxon 21 Jun 2026: 'not smashing ambition with a Capital Gains Tax'; 'New Zealand's lack of a capital gains tax is a real competitive advantage' (23 Aug 2026).

labour.evidence: 28% capital gains tax on residential investment and commercial property from 1 Jul 2027; family home, farms, shares, KiwiSaver and businesses exempt - a partial version of taxing asset gains like income.

green.evidence: Standing economic policy: 'expanding the progressive tax system to equitably tax wealth and all forms of income, such as through capital gains, land, wealth, and inheritance taxes'; 2026 wealth tax and capital acquisitions tax; criticised Labour's CGT as too limited.

act.evidence: KPMG 2026 tracker records ACT: 'No capital gains tax', 'No wealth tax/inheritance tax', tax exemption for crypto gains held over a year; ACT releases attack Labour's 'capital gains caucus' (2026). Consistent long-standing opposition.

nz-first.evidence: KPMG 2026 tracker: NZ First 'Not stated' on CGT and 'Not stated, has previously opposed such taxes' on wealth tax; Peters 13 Sep 2026 derides TOP's land tax and Green asset taxes. Inference from explicit rejection of wealth/land taxes; low.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Kiwi Tax Plan: wealth tax on net assets, 2% vacant house tax, land-banking tax, 5% stamp duty, repeal landlord interest deductibility; taxes asset holdings rather than realised gains like income - partial match.

opportunity.evidence: Land value tax of 1.75% urban/0.5% rural on unimproved land values (Tax Reset 2026) - taxes land wealth annually rather than gains as income; no CGT. Partial match.

alliance.evidence: '33% capital gains tax on realised gains, excluding the family home', covering investment property, shares and business assets, plus annual wealth tax (Tax Justice 2026).

conservative.evidence: 'Flat tax rate for individuals and for companies' and lower taxes generally; no explicit CGT statement found. Inference from explicit tax principle, low.

statements.text: Services like electricity, housing and transport are delivered better by private businesses competing than by government ownership.

national.evidence: Luxon (2025) said National is open to asset sales/'asset recycling' after the 2026 election and ruled out only state-house sales; prison redevelopment via public-private partnership (South Island Plan 2026); electricity policy opens transmission to competition. No general manifesto statement that private delivery is better, so qualified agree.

labour.evidence: NZ Future Fund: seeded state assets 'cannot be sold and will remain in public ownership for generations'; retain NZ ownership of Kiwibank; Hipkins on asset sales: 'there won't be anything left to sell'. Opposes privatisation; not an explicit claim that state delivery is better.

green.evidence: Kiwipower publicly owned electricity firm ('Public ownership'), KiwiMart public supermarket, 'tens of thousands of new public homes', replace Public Transport Operating Model so services are 'provided publicly instead of for profit'; public services and SOEs to 'remain in public hands'.

act.evidence: Electricity policy 2026: 'Open transmission to private investment'; opposes forced break-up of gentailers; cancer centres via public-private partnerships and private capital; charter schools to 10,000 places; Seymour urged a 'principle' on selling Air New Zealand (2025).

nz-first.evidence: 'Backing a New Zealand owned bank': buy back BNZ as a large state-owned bank; break up the gentailers; Peters condemns parties that 'sell our assets, privatise our country' and reports of Kiwibank/Air NZ sales (17 May 2026); 'no asset sales'.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Freshwater policy: 'Reject privatisation and trading of water rights'; energy sovereignty plan with stronger Commerce Commission/Electricity Authority powers over prices; 2,000 papakāinga and half of new social housing for whānau Māori. Opposes privatisation; not a general ownership doctrine.

opportunity.evidence: Abundant Energy: ring-fence Crown gentailer dividends and restructure the market for competition; supports Kāinga Ora plus community providers; free public transport publicly funded. Both competition and public ownership emphasised -> argued neutral.

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Fisheries policy keeps fisheries 'in public ownership' with no private sale of rights; housing policy: Ministry of Housing 'hands-on role' and restore 'leadership in social housing'. Partial, low.

alliance.evidence: Public Ownership policy (Oct 2026): 're-integrate electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and retail under public ownership'; return ports, water, telecoms and Air NZ to full public ownership; 100% publicly owned transport system; state-house rebuilding.

conservative.evidence: Mixed: 'the private sector prevailing over State control' and buying private hospital capacity, but also a state oil-tanker fleet, new state-backed refineries and a Norway-style public resource venture. Both sides -> argued neutral.

statements.text: People receiving benefits should face firm obligations and penalties for not meeting them, even if some households end up with less.

national.evidence: 'A firm, fair and affordable welfare system' (Oct 2026): lower Jobseeker rate after 2 of 3 years on benefit, drug testing with sanctions for non-compliance, 26-week stand-down for repeated voluntary unemployment; expanded Traffic Light sanctions in government (Social Security Amendment Act 2025).

labour.evidence: Labour opposed the coalition's expansion of benefit sanctions (Social Security Amendment Act 2025, Traffic Light sanctions) and National's Oct 2026 welfare package; Labour did keep obligations/sanctions when in government. Coder could not retrieve the division record - verify.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Increase benefits to liveable rates, individualise benefit entitlements and abolish benefit sanctions'; high-trust model at Work and Income; voted against Social Security Amendment Act 2025.

act.evidence: ACT welcomed the Social Security Amendment Act 2025 ('tackle benefit dependency and restore accountability'); 2026 policy: monitor spending of jobseekers on benefit over 4 months, restrict medical certification for health benefits.

nz-first.evidence: Voted for the Social Security Amendment Act 2025 (Traffic Light sanctions) as a coalition party; Peters' 2026 speeches stress 'hard work' and attack welfare dependency; no 2026 welfare manifesto found. Coalition vote, flagged.

te-pati-maori.evidence: 'Double baseline benefits - Remove sanctions and work test obligations, and cancel benefit debt owed to the Crown' (manifesto tool 2026).

opportunity.evidence: Tax Reset replaces 'most main benefits' with an unconditional Citizens' Income paid automatically, 'ending poverty traps' - removes obligations for most recipients; not framed as abolishing sanctions. Qualified disagree.

alliance.evidence: Welfare policy: 'abolish benefit sanctions', abolish stand-downs, end welfare debt recovery, Universal Benefit.

conservative.evidence: Policy index: 'Welfare: Reform is needed. Fifty years of expanding welfare has undermined our families and created an underclass'; 'Less dependency'. No specific sanctions policy; qualified.

vision-nz.evidence: 'Dismantle state dependency' and 'eliminate financial rules that disincentivise marriage' alongside 'no-strings-attached' family payments and abolishing tax on benefits. Both sides -> argued neutral, low.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Ōranga Whānau: replace 'the complex, punitive benefit system' with a non-taxable Universal Whānau Allowance, wipe $2b of MSD/IRD debt, 'Remove all relationship status policing'.

statements.text: Workers' pay and conditions are best protected by unions bargaining for whole industries, even if that raises costs for employers.

national.evidence: Repealed Fair Pay Agreements Act Dec 2023 (all National MPs voted for repeal; NZCTU scorecard Oct 2026 records National 'No' to restoring FPAs); 2026 small-business plan would require minimum employee support before collective bargaining can start.

labour.evidence: 'Fair Pay Agreements legislation introduced in the first 100 days'; 'Collective agreements the default' (Fairer Workplaces, 2026); NZCTU scorecard: Labour 'Yes' to restoring FPAs.

green.evidence: Default union membership for new workers, expanded right to strike, reverse pay-equity and Fair Pay Agreement changes (manifesto 2026); NZCTU scorecard 'Yes' to restoring FPAs.

act.evidence: Led repeal of Fair Pay Agreements (Dec 2023); 2026 small-business policy: freeze minimum wage, 'make unions collect their own fees', protect employers from personal grievances; opposes default union membership; NZCTU 'No'.

nz-first.evidence: NZCTU scorecard Oct 2026: NZ First answered 'No' to restoring Fair Pay Agreements, 'No' to opt-out union membership, 'Yes' to minimum wage above inflation; Peters: unions represent 'left wing elitist political agendas' (22 Mar 2026). Voted for FPA repeal 2023.

te-pati-maori.evidence: NZCTU scorecard Oct 2026: Te Pāti Māori 'Yes' to restoring Fair Pay Agreements and opt-out union membership; manifesto: 'stronger union rights and collective bargaining'.

opportunity.evidence: NZCTU scorecard Oct 2026: Opportunity answered 'No' to restoring Fair Pay Agreements and 'No policy' on opt-out union membership (but 'Yes' to restoring pay equity, 90-day trial abolition, living wage).

animal-justice.evidence: People policies: 'Strong unions and worker rights provide the foundation for reducing inequality'; worker rights 'through collective organisation'. No FPA/industry-bargaining specifics; qualified.

alliance.evidence: Workers' Rights policy: 'Restore national collective bargaining', broad right to strike, Work Councils; NZCTU scorecard Oct 2026: Alliance 'Yes' to restoring Fair Pay Agreements.

womens-rights.evidence: 'reinstatement of legislative support for Fair Pay Agreements' and pay equity in private and public sectors (full policy 2025).

statements.text: Keeping government debt low should take priority over spending more on health and education right now.

national.evidence: Budget Responsibility Rules (9 Aug 2026): 'prioritising a return to surplus in 2028/29', 'bending debt down below 40% of GDP'; 'books in surplus so we don't saddle our kids with more debt'. Also commits to continuing health/education investment, so qualified agree.

labour.evidence: Fiscal Strategy: surplus by 2029/30 and net debt 'around 20% of GDP over time', but 'You can't cut your way to growth'; prioritises Medicard, hospital repairs and school upgrades now. Qualified disagree.

green.evidence: Standing policy: 'Enabling greater government borrowing for investing in infrastructure'; manifesto reforms public finance to 'support long-term resilience... health and well-being'; Green Budget 2025 funded by taxes on wealth, not spending restraint.

act.evidence: balancethebooks.nz / Fiscal Plan 2026: 'ACT will pay down debt faster', reduce operating allowance, keep NZ Super Fund contributions suspended, raise super age to 67; spending to 2017 levels.

nz-first.evidence: Peters attacks Labour's 'massive debt' and the Greens' '$88 billion debt increase' but proposes a $100b NZ Future Fund, $1b oil and gas survey and $5,000 Kiwi Kids grants; no fiscal rule stated. Both sides -> argued neutral.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Manifesto 2026 commits to large new spending (doubled benefits, free GP and dental, $4.5b Oranga Whenua fund, $1.25b kura property) funded by new taxes; no debt target; Peters criticises its scale. Spending prioritised over debt.

opportunity.evidence: Intergenerational Infrastructure (2026): 'New Zealand... can borrow carefully'; 'New Zealand's balance sheet is strong'; raise up to $60b for infrastructure; health to 9% of GDP. Spending on investment prioritised over debt reduction; qualified.

alliance.evidence: Platform of universal free health care, child benefit, 52 weeks' parental leave and public job creation funded by new taxes; 'full employment' and public investment as central goals; no debt-reduction target.

conservative.evidence: 'debt levels are a crisis which needs to be addressed now'; 'urgently tackling the massive debt'; but spending to be redirected to infrastructure and hospital waiting lists. Qualified agree.

statements.text: People who commit serious crimes should be given longer prison sentences, even if it means more people in prison for longer at public expense.

national.evidence: Voted for Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act (3rd reading 13 Dec 2024) and sentencing-discount caps; campaign launch 27 Sep 2026: 'locking offenders up for longer to keep our community safe'; 240 extra prison beds at Christchurch Men's Prison.

labour.evidence: Voted against Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act (Dec 2024; Duncan Webb: minimum-sentence laws 'did little to reduce serious crime'); no 2026 pledge to repeal.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Enable judicial discretion in sentencing, including by abolishing mandatory minimum sentences, life sentences, preventive detention, limits on sentence discounts, three strikes'; voted against Three Strikes 2024.

act.evidence: Three Strikes for repeat burglars: minimum three-year sentence on third conviction (2026 policy); sponsored Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act 2024 (Nicole McKee).

nz-first.evidence: Law and order policy (Oct 2026): 'Life means life' whole-of-life sentences for first-degree murder and child rape, more mandatory minimums, tougher parole, limits on sentence discounts; voted for Three Strikes 2024.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Justice manifesto 2026: 'Abolish prisons by 2040', repeal three strikes, gang and bail laws, Māori Justice Authority funded from half the Corrections/Police/Courts budgets; voted against Three Strikes 2024.

opportunity.evidence: 'Smart on Crime' (2026): fund rehabilitation and prevention from the Corrections budget; cites $200,000 per prisoner; redirect boot-camp funding; no sentencing-length policy. Qualified disagree.

legalise-cannabis.evidence: Policy redirects enforcement money 'to fight serious crime' but argues 'criminalisation is self-perpetuating' and seeks a prohibition truth-and-reconciliation commission; no sentencing-length position. Weak inference, low.

alliance.evidence: Justice policy: 'Our high imprisonment rate cannot be addressed simply by building more prisons or imposing harsher sentences'; 'reduce unnecessary imprisonment', 'three strikes and into treatment'.

conservative.evidence: Principles: 'Punishment that will deter crime. Removal of criminals from society'; child-protection policy: 'repeat child sexual offenders face significantly longer prison sentences', review sentence reductions; overview: 'meaningful consequences for serious and repeat offending'.

womens-rights.evidence: Supports 'standalone, sex-based laws with higher penalties' for violence against women and children, banning the rough-sex defence, keeping biological males out of women's prisons. Partial - longer sentences only for this class of crime; low.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Te Hokinga Mai: 'Prison Sinking Lid Policy' diverting non-violent offenders into hapū-run rehabilitation; prisons 'perpetuate multi-generational trauma'.

statements.text: Police should have more power to stop, search and move people on in public places, even if that limits some civil liberties.

national.evidence: Government bill creating police move-on orders passed final reading 18 Sep 2026 (Justice Minister Goldsmith); Gangs Act 2024 (patch ban, dispersal notices) passed 68-55 with National support.

labour.evidence: Voted against the Gangs Act 2024 but later said it would not repeal the patch ban; on the 2026 move-on orders bill Labour sought amendments to protect rough sleepers rather than opposing the power outright (3 Sep 2026 release). Both sides emphasised -> argued neutral.

green.evidence: Voted against Gangs Act 2024 (dispersal and non-consorting powers 'would increase racism and the incarceration of Māori'); opposed the 2026 move-on orders bill entirely; manifesto: body cameras, stronger IPCA.

act.evidence: Voted for Gangs Act 2024 and the 2026 move-on orders bill; 2026 policy to licence security professionals with 'more authority against intrusion or theft' and expand rural policing. ACT's civil-liberties framing (opposed some search powers in the past) makes this qualified.

nz-first.evidence: Voted for Gangs Act 2024 and the 2026 move-on orders bill; Oct 2026 policy: dedicated organised-crime agency, fold SFO into Police; Peters campaigns on 'law and order on our streets'.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Justice manifesto 2026: repeal gang laws, body cameras for all police, replace the IPCA with a genuinely independent body; voted against Gangs Act 2024 (Waititi: would 'discriminate against Māori people').

statements.text: Adults should be free to make their own choices about things like drug use, even if others consider those choices harmful or wrong.

national.evidence: Luxon (7 Oct 2022): National 'won't decriminalise cannabis'; 2026 welfare policy introduces drug testing of beneficiaries with sanctions. No newer general statement found; older statement used as nothing newer exists.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Repeal and replace the Misuse of Drugs Act... treats drug use as a health issue and provides for regulated access to cannabis for personal use'; psychedelic licensing; Good Samaritan laws.

act.evidence: No 2026 drug-law policy; ACT welcomed benefit drug-testing and supported the 2025 drug-driving law; Seymour's 2020 referendum stance was personal. Coded -1 low from ACT's support for coercive drug measures in government; flagged as weak.

nz-first.evidence: NZ First opposed the 2020 cannabis legalisation referendum and in 2026 campaigns on 'conservative values' and informed consent in health; no 2026 drug-law policy. Inference from its 2020 position (older evidence, nothing newer found), low.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Justice manifesto 2026: 'Decriminalise drug use' and treat it as a health issue.

opportunity.evidence: 'Decriminalise drug possession, but not supply'; 'Support moves to legalise and regulate recreational use of cannabis' (Smart on Crime 2026).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Cannabis policy: no criminal offence for personal possession or growing; Direct Democracy page lists 'bodily autonomy' and 'the right to refuse medical treatment' among sacred rights.

legalise-cannabis.evidence: Full Spectrum Policy: 'possession, cultivation and use of pure cannabis... be free from prosecution', regulated R18 commerce, expunge convictions; principle of 'upholding of individual and civic rights where these do not unreasonably impinge on others'.

statements.text: Schools and public institutions should reflect changing social attitudes about gender, sexuality and family, even if some parents and communities object.

national.evidence: Health Minister Simeon Brown (National) halted new puberty-blocker prescriptions from 19 Dec 2025 (announced 19 Nov 2025); Education Minister Stanford's 2025 relationships and sexuality framework emphasises parental consultation/opt-out. Government actions attributable to National ministers; flagged.

labour.evidence: Labour rainbow spokesperson Shanan Halbert called the Nov 2025 puberty-blocker ban 'one of the most damaging and ideological moves'; 2026 policy for a rainbow health strategy. No explicit position on the 2025 RSE framework found.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Restore relationship and sexuality teaching guidelines - including education on... diverse identities and sexualities... in all schools'; reverse the puberty-blocker ban; amend Human Rights Act for gender identity.

act.evidence: ACT children's spokesperson Karen Chhour 'backs moves to prioritise child safety' - welcomed the Nov 2025 suspension of new puberty-blocker prescriptions; ACT policy to increase private-school subsidies and parental choice; opposed Labour-era RSE guidelines.

nz-first.evidence: Peters 19 Jul 2026: 'We have taken men out of women's sports. We stopped the use of puberty blockers in children'; member's bill to define 'woman' and 'man' biologically; coalition removal of Labour-era RSE guidelines; repeal DEI requirements bill.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Mana Takatāpui policy (23 Sep 2026): $200m, Takatāpui-governed Commission, 'gender affirming kaupapa Māori healthcare', protection from hate; te reo and tikanga compulsory in schools. No explicit RSE statement found; strong direction.

opportunity.evidence: State of the Nation 2026 defends 'transgender Kiwis' against NZ First's 'policies of fear and division'; no RSE or gender-health policy found. Inferred from an explicit principle, low.

nz-loyal.evidence: Website platform as quoted by RNZ (12 Oct 2026): 'Protect our children from corrupt sex and gender education'. Party site not retrievable.

alliance.evidence: Women and Gender Equality policy: 'support for informed-consent gender-affirming care', Gender Audit framework; no schools/RSE statement. Qualified agree.

conservative.evidence: 'Protecting children from radical gender ideology'; 'A man is a man, and a woman is a woman'; restrict gender-related medical procedures for minors with parental involvement.

womens-rights.evidence: Full policy (4 Nov 2025): stop schools supporting 'social transition', full disclosure to parents of sexuality education, sex-based rights 'given precedence over any proposed provisions based on concepts of gender'; ban puberty blockers for under-18s.

vision-nz.evidence: 'Completely remove ideologically driven gender theory, Relationship and Sexuality Education (RSE), and political propaganda from the national curriculum'; ban gender-transition interventions for minors; Parental Rights Bill (Our Policies, 2026).

statements.text: People should be free to say what they think in public and online, even if others find it offensive or harmful.

national.evidence: In government National passed the Education and Training Amendment Act 2025 requiring universities to protect free speech and dropped Labour's hate-speech law work (ACT coalition commitments); but Luxon's 2026 policy bans under-16s from social media. Coalition-driven, qualified agree, flagged.

labour.evidence: 2026 'Safer Online' policy: Digital Duty of Care requiring platforms to protect people from 'harmful content', independent online regulator with fining powers, under-16 social media ban. (Hate-speech law work was dropped in 2023.) Qualified disagree.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Extend hate speech laws to cover religion, gender, disability and rainbow communities'; Digital Duty of Care regulating harmful online content.

act.evidence: 2026 policy 'Professional free speech': stop professionals being disciplined for opinions expressed outside practice; secured university free-speech law (Education and Training Amendment Act 2025) and scrapping of hate-speech law work in the coalition agreement; 'Prevent any banning of VPNs'.

nz-first.evidence: Peters attacks 'woke cancel culture' and political correctness (22 Aug 2026); NZ First supported the coalition's university free-speech law and scrapping hate-speech work; but also promotes a social-media/misinformation posture (opposes under-16 ban). Qualified agree.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Mana Takatāpui policy seeks 'protection from violence and hate'; party backed hate-speech criminalisation in 2021 and sought Speaker action against 'racist and hateful' remarks (Oct 2024). No 2026 hate-speech law pledge found; qualified disagree.

opportunity.evidence: Clean Up Politics: prohibit materially inaccurate statements of fact in electoral advertisements, defended as a 'modest' limit on speech; supports under-16 social media bill to select committee. Qualified disagree, low.

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Enshrine NZBORA as supreme law so 'freedom of speech, movement, thought and conscience' can never be 'voted away by politicians' (Sue Grey).

animal-justice.evidence: Policy summary: 'whistleblower protection and support for peaceful protest' - protects dissent but not offensive speech generally; low.

conservative.evidence: 'Freedom of speech and assembly' (What We Stand For); 'Defend freedom of speech and assembly' (policies); overview: free to 'express their views, practise their beliefs'; laws 'must not be weaponised to target people with particular views'.

womens-rights.evidence: Hate Crimes proposal: 'The Women's Rights Party does not support the creation of new hate crime laws'; concern that such laws 'could lead to a crackdown' on women's-rights advocacy. Opposes new speech crimes; qualified agree.

statements.text: Young people who offend should face tougher consequences rather than mainly being supported through welfare and youth services.

national.evidence: Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill creating Young Serious Offender declarations and military-style academies passed under urgency with National's votes; National's 2026 law-and-order material claims 'youth offending down 26%' and ram raids down 85% as results of tougher approach.

labour.evidence: 'Stop running youth offender boot camps' / 'National must scrap its failed boot camps' (2026); voted against military-style academies legislation.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'End military-style academies, raise the age of criminal responsibility'; expand Rangatahi Courts and rehabilitation; voted against the bootcamps bill.

act.evidence: ACT minister Karen Chhour sponsored the Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill creating Young Serious Offender declarations and military-style academies (passed 2026); 2026 policy gives teachers powers to remove disruptive students. Government action by an ACT minister, flagged.

nz-first.evidence: Voted for the military-style academies (bootcamps) legislation as a coalition party; Peters' speeches cite ram raids and youth crime under Labour. No NZ First-specific youth-justice policy found; coalition vote flagged.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Justice manifesto 2026: 'close military-style bootcamps and youth justice residences', raise the age of criminal responsibility to 16; Mokopuna Māori Authority to replace state care.

opportunity.evidence: Smart on Crime 2026: redirect funding from 'demonstrably ineffective programmes like the current government's boot camps' to prevention, whānau-centred interventions for persistent young offenders and rehabilitation.

alliance.evidence: Justice policy: habilitation centres 'particularly for young people', Community Care Orders, iwi-run rehabilitation for young offenders instead of imprisonment.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Māori Justice & Autonomous Policing Act: transfer youth-justice budgets to iwi-governed authorities, 'restorative justice networks' replacing 'punitive policing and incarceration'.

statements.text: Te Tiriti o Waitangi should continue to shape our laws and how public services are run, even if that means some decisions are made differently for Māori.

national.evidence: Campaign launch 27 Sep 2026: health minister 'with the guts to end Labour's obsession with co-governance'; coalition policy of targeting services 'by need not race'; Treaty clauses review (coalition commitment). National voted against the Treaty Principles Bill (10 Apr 2025), so not strongly disagree.

labour.evidence: Will restore the Te Tiriti obligation on school boards (21 May 2026), restore Mana Whakahono a Rohe iwi participation agreements, partner with Māori in education after Tribunal findings (17 Sep 2026); Greenpeace Q21 'Yes' to Treaty clauses in environmental law.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Implement genuine Te Tiriti-based decision-making models across government and resource iwi and hapū to participate as partners'; Te Tiriti clauses in environment law (Greenpeace Q21 'Yes').

act.evidence: 'One Law for All' policy 2026: 'scale back the use and effect of Treaty principles in legislation', remove ethnicity-based criteria for public services; promoted the Treaty Principles Bill (voted for at second reading 10 Apr 2025).

nz-first.evidence: Greenpeace 2026 answer: 'our policy is to remove references to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi from environmental laws, including the RMA'; Treaty clauses review in coalition agreement; Peters: 'racist co-governance' (19 Jul 2026).

te-pati-maori.evidence: Te Tiriti Entrenchment policy (1 Sep 2026): Te Tiriti Impact Statement for every Bill, $220m Mātike Mai Fund, constitutional transformation by 2040; Greenpeace Q21 'Yes'.

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Direct Democracy: Swiss-style binding citizens' veto and citizen-initiated laws with low signature thresholds; 'the power of veto shifts entirely to you'; demand a binding referendum on direct democracy as a coalition condition.

animal-justice.evidence: People policies praise deliberative democracy (Irish citizens' assembly leading to a referendum) and propose citizens' assemblies; not binding referendums per se. Qualified, low.

alliance.evidence: Constitutional review to 'examine the establishment of Citizens' Initiatives, allowing citizens to propose legislation'; referendum on the monarchy; 'Any constitutional change should be determined democratically by the people'. Qualified agree.

conservative.evidence: 'Honest democratic process' and 'give power back to the people' with reforms aimed at bureaucrats and judiciary rather than referendums; no referendum policy. Vague -> argued neutral, low.

vision-nz.evidence: Democracy Reset: abolish MMP party lists, cut MP numbers, term limits - reforms of representative democracy, not referendums; 'Reject the introduction of digital IDs'. No referendum policy; weak inference, low.

statements.text: Only individual voters on the electoral roll should be allowed to donate to political parties, even if parties then have less money to campaign.

labour.evidence: Greenpeace Q24 (voters-only donations): 'Labour believes in transparent and fair rules for political party donations' - no commitment; 2026 policy only extends disclosure to third-party campaigners. Vague -> argued neutral.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Reform electoral funding by limiting donations to registered voters, increasing public financing of campaigns and capping a donor's donations'; Greenpeace Q24 'Yes'.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Greenpeace Q24 (only registered voters can donate): 'Yes'.

opportunity.evidence: Clean Up Politics: 'Ban donations from companies and trusts, so only registered New Zealand voters can donate', cap at $30,000 per donor; Greenpeace Q24 'Yes'.

animal-justice.evidence: People policies: 'Permit only New Zealand citizens or permanent residents registered to vote to make political donations, removing corporate/industry entity donations'; $30,000 cap per cycle; disclosure threshold $1,500.

alliance.evidence: 'strict transparency requirements for political donations... consider appropriate limits on political donations to prevent wealthy individuals, corporations, and other organisations from acquiring disproportionate political influence'; not an individuals-only rule. Qualified.

statements.text: Local councils should be free to make their own decisions, even if rates and rules then differ from place to place, rather than central government overriding them.

national.evidence: Rates Capping Bill: councils' annual rate rises held to a 2-4% target range with an independent regulator (policy page, 2026); Government also required binding polls on Māori wards (2024).

labour.evidence: Voted against the 2024 law overriding council decisions on Māori wards by forcing binding polls (Hipkins: coalition 'embarrassing' NZ). No stated 2026 position on the rates cap found in sources checked; +1 inferred from that vote only, flagged.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Reject the proposed rates cap and enable a range of new funding and financing tools'; 'empower councils by devolving further responsibilities'; reinstate councils' ability to keep Māori wards.

act.evidence: Mixed: 'Local Tourism Dividend' gives councils $1 per visitor night and ACT opposes a bed tax that councils want; 'No votes for unelected reps' and binding Māori-ward polls override council choices; 'Make councils pay fair compensation' for overlays. Both centralising and devolving -> argued neutral.

nz-first.evidence: Fluoridation decisions returned to local communities by referendum, but NZ First backed central overrides: binding Māori-ward polls, disestablishing the IMSB, pausing Waikato Regional Council's Plan Change 1 and the coalition rates cap. Both sides -> argued neutral.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Would require Māori wards and mana whenua representation 'in all councils' (central mandate) while giving hapū and iwi the same disaster resources as councils and opposing coalition overrides. Mixed -> argued neutral.

opportunity.evidence: Intergenerational Infrastructure: 'Arbitrary, central government-imposed rate[s caps]' criticised; expand council funding tools and GST share; but an independent regulator would hold councils to asset-management standards. Qualified agree.

nz-loyal.evidence: 'Decentralise government and return power to the people' (website via RNZ, Oct 2026) - general principle covering council autonomy; inference, low.

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: 'Subsidiarity': decisions on local infrastructure, land management and regional development 'returned entirely to local communities'; regions retain a portion of GST and tax raised locally.

alliance.evidence: Constitutional review to consider 'the role of local government'; end requirement for councils to put water into arms-length entities; repeal procurement rules forcing councils into corporatised public transport. Qualified agree.

conservative.evidence: Principles: 'Decision-making should be as local as possible... localism'; 'Local decision making'; mayors may become full-time council CEOs; ministers to appoint and sack senior officials. Qualified agree.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Decentralised, rohe-based delivery of health, justice and civil defence; deregulation of hyper-local food trade 'free of council licensing'. Supports local autonomy generally though not councils specifically; inference, low.
